question: What is the primary physical characteristic of a convulsion?
explanation: Convulsions involve sudden, involuntary, and rapid shaking movements caused by uncontrolled muscle contractions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h1)

question: Why should a nurse avoid using 'seizure' and 'convulsion' as exact synonyms?

options.A: Seizures are always caused by low blood sugar
options.B: Convulsions only occur in pediatric patients
options.C: Convulsions cannot be managed with medication
options.D: Not all seizures involve physical muscle shaking

explanation: Many types of seizures cause behavioral changes or staring spells without physical convulsions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h1)

question: Which neurotransmitter is primarily responsible for inhibitory control in the brain?
explanation: GABA acts as the main inhibitory neurotransmitter to prevent excessive electrical firing in neurons. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h2)

question: What happens at the cellular level during the onset of a convulsion?

options.A: Cerebral blood flow increases to maximum capacity
options.B: Neurons fire in an excessive and synchronized manner
options.C: Brain cells undergo rapid programmed cell death
options.D: Neuronal electrical activity drops to zero

explanation: Convulsions start when a group of neurons fire abnormally and synchronize their electrical impulses. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h2)

question: A seizure that starts in one specific area of the brain and spreads to both hemispheres is classified as what?
explanation: This type begins focally before recruiting both hemispheres into a generalized convulsion. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h3)

question: How do focal motor seizures differ primarily from generalized motor seizures?

options.A: Generalized seizures affect only one limb at a time
options.B: Focal seizures never involve any physical shaking movements
options.C: Focal seizures start in a specific, localized region of one hemisphere
options.D: Generalized seizures always result in permanent brain damage

explanation: Focal seizures originate in a localized network within a single hemisphere, unlike generalized ones. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h3)

question: Which metabolic imbalance is a well-known systemic trigger for convulsions?
explanation: Low blood sugar starves brain cells of energy, destabilizing membranes and triggering convulsions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h4)

question: What is the primary mechanism by which severe high fever causes convulsions in infants?

options.A: Fever increases red blood cell production rapidly
options.B: High body temperature permanently destroys brain tissue
options.C: Rapid temperature elevation lowers the neurological seizure threshold
options.D: Excessive sweating causes severe whole-body dehydration

explanation: Rapidly rising temperatures make immature infant neurons more prone to firing electrical storms. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h4)

question: What term describes the recovery period immediately following a convulsive episode?
explanation: The post-ictal phase is the recovery period where the patient experiences drowsiness, confusion, and exhaustion. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h5)

question: Why is precise timing of a convulsive episode critical during nursing assessment?

options.A: It determines the exact blood glucose level of the patient
options.B: It dictates the precise nutritional requirements for recovery
options.C: It prevents the occurrence of future febrile episodes
options.D: It helps differentiate standard seizures from prolonged status epilepticus

explanation: Seizures lasting beyond five minutes signal status epilepticus, requiring immediate emergency intervention. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h5)

question: Which diagnostic tool directly records the electrical activity of the brain?
explanation: An EEG measures and records electrical voltage fluctuations generated by brain neurons. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h6)

question: Why is a lumbar puncture performed in some patients presenting with new-onset convulsions?

options.A: To measure the exact oxygen saturation of brain tissue
options.B: To check cerebrospinal fluid for signs of meningitis or infection
options.C: To relieve intracranial pressure inside the ventricles
options.D: To inject anticonvulsant medications directly into the spinal cord

explanation: Analyzing cerebrospinal fluid helps rule out life-threatening central nervous system infections. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h6)

question: What is the correct immediate nursing action when a patient begins to convulse in bed?

options.A: Force a padded tongue depressor between teeth
options.B: Attempt to sit the patient upright immediately
options.C: Restrain all four limbs tightly to prevent injury
options.D: Gently turn the patient onto their side

explanation: Turning the patient to the side keeps the airway clear and prevents aspiration of secretions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h7)

question: What is the primary reason for avoiding hard objects in a convulsing patient's mouth?

options.A: It leads to permanent tongue paralysis
options.B: It accelerates the spread of infection
options.C: It can fracture teeth and obstruct the airway
options.D: It causes immediate cessation of breathing

explanation: Forceful insertion of objects during spasms damages teeth and creates choking hazards. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h7)

question: Which medication class is standard for stopping an acute, ongoing convulsion?
explanation: Benzodiazepines act quickly on GABA receptors to suppress acute seizure activity. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h8)

question: What vital instruction must a nurse give to a patient starting maintenance anti-seizure drugs?

options.A: Double the dose whenever feeling stressed or anxious
options.B: Never stop taking the medication suddenly without medical guidance
options.C: Take the tablets only when a seizure aura approaches
options.D: Stop the drug immediately if minor drowsiness occurs

explanation: Abrupt withdrawal of anti-seizure drugs frequently triggers severe rebound convulsions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h8)

question: How long must continuous seizure activity last to be classified as status epilepticus?
explanation: Seizures persisting beyond five minutes without cessation are classified as status epilepticus. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h9)

question: Why is status epilepticus considered a critical medical emergency?

options.A: Prolonged seizure activity causes severe hypoxia and brain damage
options.B: Patients develop permanent paralysis in all four limbs
options.C: Blood pressure drops to zero within the first minute
options.D: It always results from a minor vitamin deficiency

explanation: Uncontrolled continuous firing starves the brain of oxygen and glucose, risking permanent injury. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T10#GNS222_U4_T10_h9)
